All walkthroughs / Harbour Clinic

Harbour Clinic · Closing an organisation

Hand over a closed clinic's records for a legal case

A court demands a patient’s appointment records from a clinic that is closing down, and a legal hold already keeps them. One platform administrator asks for them, a different one approves, and the custodian the hold names confirms what is included and names the patient, so that only that patient’s rows leave. The platform builds a package that is signed and encrypted, and the custodian alone is given the passphrase. The recipient opens it on their own computer with a program that checks it.

How to read this page

  • Every step names the tool or the part of Munitas where it happens. The label under the title says where, and the step reads in the same order each time: what is happening, the evidence, and then what to look for in it.
  • Console steps happen in the Munitas console, the web app that people open in a browser. They show real screenshots, and clicking one enlarges it.
  • Python steps happen in Python, on the person’s own computer, in a notebook or in a terminal. Python is a window where a person types a line and sees the answer straight away. From there the person uses the Munitas client library, which sends requests to Munitas, and DuckDB, a free tool for analysing tables. Each dark box on the page is one of these steps.
  • In a dark box, the top part is exactly what was typed and the bottom part is exactly what came back. me is the client library signed in as the person named on the label, and custodian is the client library signed in as the custodian.
  • Every step was run for real by a script that types each one, so the answers are genuine and nothing has been edited. Every name of a person, patient or card holder in the example data is invented.

Words used on this page

Organisation
A company or hospital group that uses Munitas. Each organisation sees only its own data.
Department
A team inside an organisation that owns some of its data, such as Cardiology.
Dataset
A named collection of records, such as a table of patient admissions.
Sealed
Finished and closed for good, so that it can never be edited.
Custodian
A person who holds the data custodian role, which allows deciding who may read data. A custodian decides for the departments they are an approver for.
Platform administrator
The person who runs Munitas itself. The role gives no say over who may read any department’s data.
Legal hold
An instruction from a court, a regulator or a law firm to keep an organisation’s records and not delete them while a legal matter is open.
Temporary custodian
The person a legal hold names to answer for the kept records while the hold stands. The person confirms having read the notice.
Data protection officer
A person who watches how an organisation handles personal data. The role decides nothing about who may read it.
Export for a legal matter
Producing some of an organisation’s kept records for a court, a regulator or a law firm that has demanded them. It needs a legal hold in force and three different people.
Filter
Keeping only the rows of a table that match values the custodian names, such as one patient’s id, so that other people’s rows do not leave with them.
Manifest
The list of every file in a package, each with its size and a fingerprint of its contents. The platform signs it, so that changing a file or the list can be noticed.
Passphrase
A long secret that opens an encrypted file. It travels separately from the file, so that having the file alone is not enough.
Fingerprint
A value worked out from the exact contents of a file. It changes if even one byte changes, so it shows that a file was not altered.
Claim
A statement, made by the person who brings a dataset in, about how sensitive it is. A different approver of the owning department has to confirm it.
Version
One sealed state of a dataset. Changing the contents means making a new version, never editing an old one.
Closing down an organisation
Ending an organisation’s use of Munitas in two stages of 15 days. In the first its people can read and may cancel. In the second they can do nothing. When both end, everything inside the organisation is deleted.

PART ONE

A court demands the records

This story starts where the walkthrough about closing down an organisation ends. Harbour Clinic is closing down, and a legal hold is in force on it. A legal hold is an order to keep an organisation’s records and not delete them. It only keeps them. Now the High Court has demanded the appointment records of the patient who is making the claim, Ms Alder, together with the log of who read them. The clinic’s appointments are one table of ten rows, covering five patients, so handing over the whole table would send four other patients’ records out with it. Producing records is a different act from keeping them, so the platform gives it its own steps. Three different people each do one step, and none of them reads the records. Priya is a platform administrator, a person who runs Munitas itself and who has no say over who may read any department’s data. To start this story the clinic was closed down through the platform and the first 15 days were skipped by a script run by an administrator, which moves the clinic’s two closing dates back and changes nothing else. The dates on the screens are therefore earlier than they would be on a real calendar.

1
Priya
Priya finds the legal hold in force, and a way to ask for records
Munitas console · Legal holds · /legal-holds, the hold in force on harbour

Under every legal hold that is in force there is a section called Producing records for this matter. A hold that is only waiting for approval, or that has been released, has no such section, because the platform produces records only while a hold stands. The section repeats the three steps in one sentence before it offers anything.

The card for HC-2026-0417: Alder v Harbour Clinic carries the red label In force. Below the notice, the section Producing records for this matter holds one button, Ask for records to be produced. The sentence under the heading reads Nobody reads the records: the platform builds an encrypted, signed package.
2
Priya
Priya copies the demand into the form, and chooses to hand over only the claimant’s rows
Munitas console · Legal holds · the request form under the hold

The form asks for what the court sent, in the court’s words: who is demanding the records, the reference of the demand, its date, and what it asks for. It also asks who receives the package. Then Priya chooses which datasets are included. A dataset is the platform’s name for a registered, named collection of records. Choosing a dataset includes every sealed version of it, and a sealed version is a finished state of a dataset that can never be edited. A dataset that is a table offers a second choice: hand over the whole table, or only the rows for named people, matched on one column. Priya chooses the second. Priya does not name the people. The custodian does, in a later step, because the custodian answers for the records.

The fields read: demanded by High Court, King’s Bench Division, reference KB-2026-004411, recipient Ruth Aldous of Aldous and Brennan LLP. Only appointments is ticked, marked a table, and its choice reads only the rows for named people, matched on patient_id. The line beside it reads The custodian names the people when confirming. The audit trail is ticked too.
3
Priya
The request is recorded, and it waits for a second administrator
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter

Nothing has been built yet. The request is stored with who asked and when, and it waits for a different platform administrator. The first thing it records is the audit trail, the permanent list of every decision the platform makes, so the request itself is evidence that somebody asked.

A card with the demand’s reference KB-2026-004411 carries the amber label Waiting for a second administrator. It lists Demanded by, Asks for, Goes to and Asked for by Priya. Under the buttons: You asked for this one, so a different administrator approves it.
4
Priya
Priya presses Approve on the request that Priya made, and is refused
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter

The page draws the Approve button for every platform administrator, and the platform decides when it is pressed. It refuses the person who asked. The same rule is written into the database as a check, so a fault in the program could not bypass it. The refusal is also written to the audit trail.

A red panel reads Could not decide this export and gives the reason an export is approved by a different platform administrator from the one who asked for it. The status is unchanged, still Waiting for a second administrator.
PART TWO

A second platform administrator approves it

Ravi is the second platform administrator. Ravi and Priya hold the same role, and the rule is only that the two are different people.

5
Ravi
Ravi reads the demand and writes a note
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter

Ravi sees the same waiting request with the whole demand in front of the decision. The note is stored with the decision. It is required only when a request is declined.

The name at the bottom left of the menu is Ravi. The note field reads Demand checked against the court’s reference, and both Approve it and Decline are offered. There is no line saying that Ravi asked for this one.
6
Ravi
Ravi approves, and the request moves to the custodian
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter

Approval is the second of three steps. The platform administrators have done their part, and nothing is built yet, because the person who answers for the records has not confirmed what is included.

The label now reads Waiting for the custodian to confirm the scope, and the card adds Approved by Ravi with the note.
PART THREE

The custodian names the claimant, and is given the passphrase

Adeyemi is the clinic’s data protection officer, and the legal hold names Adeyemi as its temporary custodian, the person who answers for the kept records while the hold stands. The clinic is in its second stage, so the usual screens are closed to Adeyemi. The one thing still open is what concerns the hold.

7
Adeyemi
Adeyemi is asked to confirm the scope, and to name the people
Munitas console · Closing notice · shown in place of every other screen

Besides the hold, the notice now shows the export that waits for the custodian. The custodian sees the whole demand, who asked and who approved. Only the custodian can confirm that what is asked for matches the demand and goes no further, because the custodian answers for the records. Neither platform administrator can. For a table that is filtered there is one more thing only the custodian does: name the people the demand is about.

A box titled Records being produced for a legal matter holds the card KB-2026-004411: matter HC-2026-0417. It says Filtered: appointments, Only the rows for named people, matched on the column patient_id. The custodian names them. A box below asks for one value of the column patient_id per line and says that the platform administrators never see these values.
8
Adeyemi
Adeyemi names the claimant, and checks how many rows match
Munitas console · Closing notice · Records being produced for a legal matter

Adeyemi types the claimant’s patient id, P-4471, which is the value the table uses for Ms Alder. The platform matches a value exactly, as written. Before confirming, Adeyemi presses a button to check how many rows match. The answer is a count and nothing else: the rows are not shown, and a value that matches no row would be listed by name, so that a mistyped id does not quietly produce an empty package.

The box holds P-4471. Under it: 2 of 10 rows match. The note field reads Ms Alder’s patient id, and nothing more, and the button The scope is right is usable. Without a value in the box it would stay greyed out.
9
Adeyemi
The package is built, and the passphrase is waiting
Munitas console · Closing notice · Records being produced for a legal matter

Confirming starts a background job. It copies the files of the named datasets, checks each one against the fingerprint recorded when it was sealed, and writes them into one package that it signs and encrypts. For the filtered table it reads the table and keeps only the rows that match, and it includes nothing else of that table: not the original records, and not the copy of the table that holds every row. No person opens the package, and no platform administrator can, because the secret that opens it, called a passphrase, is held back for the custodian.

The label reads Ready. The card adds Scope confirmed by Adeyemi, the line 2 of 10 rows matched and no patient id, Package reading 1 file, its size and encrypted, and Kept until Oct 25, 2026, after which the platform deletes the package. A button reads Show me the passphrase, once.
10
Adeyemi
Adeyemi reads the passphrase, once
Munitas console · Closing notice · Records being produced for a legal matter

The passphrase is shown on this screen and nowhere else. The platform does not keep it after this, so it cannot be shown again and cannot be recovered. The custodian passes it to the recipient separately from the download link, so that holding the file alone is not enough to open it.

A yellow box shows the passphrase, five groups of letters and digits, and the line Shown once and not kept. Give it to the recipient separately from the download link. The button has gone.
PART FOUR

A platform administrator makes the download link

Delivery is a person’s act, because how a court or a law firm wants to receive a package is not the platform’s decision. The platform makes a package available and records every download.

11
Priya
Priya sees what the package holds, without opening it
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter, with the list of files

A platform administrator never sees the records, but sees what is in the package. The list is called the manifest. It names every file and gives its size and a fingerprint of its contents, which is a value that changes if even one byte of the file changes. The platform signs the manifest, so any later change to a file or to the list can be noticed.

The status is Ready. The card says Filtered: appointments, Only the rows for named people, matched on the column patient_id and 2 of 10 rows matched, and it shows no patient id. The table lists one file, data/appointments/v1/v1.filtered.csv, with its size and the start of its SHA-256 fingerprint. The button Make a download link is below the table.
12
Priya
Priya makes a download link
Munitas console · Legal holds · Producing records for this matter

The link is shown once. It works three times and for seven days at most, and each use is written to the audit trail. The package is encrypted, so the link alone opens nothing. The recipient also needs the passphrase that only Adeyemi was given.

A box under the button shows the link, beginning with the platform’s address and /legal-exports/download/mlx_, and the line Works 3 times until Oct 18, 2026. It is not shown again.
PART FIVE

The recipient opens the package

Ruth Aldous is a lawyer at the firm that is to receive the package. The platform has finished its part. Ruth has been sent the link and, separately, the passphrase, and works on Ruth’s own computer with a small program that comes with Munitas, open_legal_package.py. The program shares no code with the platform, so that the format of the package is the only thing the two have in common. What follows was recorded by running the real commands. The link and the passphrase are shown as placeholders here, because they are secrets.

13
Ruth Aldous
Ruth asks the platform for the key that signs its packages
Terminal · on the recipient’s computer

The platform publishes the public half of its signing key. A public key lets anybody check a signature and lets nobody make one. Ruth asks for it directly from the platform, so that the check below does not rest on anything that came inside the package.

Typed by Ruth, in a terminal on the recipient's computer
curl <the platform's address>/legal-exports/signing-key
What came back
{"algorithm":"ed25519","public_key":"2bdeb5795b70f451b6a0152fd0dc508a06eb522f1f6f23424e770c5652d3c238"}
The answer names the algorithm, ed25519, and gives the key as a long string of letters and digits.
14
Ruth Aldous
Ruth downloads the package and opens it
Terminal · on the recipient’s computer

The first command saves the file the link hands over. The second decrypts it with the passphrase, unpacks it, and checks three things: the manifest’s signature against the platform’s key, every file against the size and fingerprint in the manifest, and that no file is present that the manifest does not list. Any failure makes the program say so and stop.

Typed by Ruth, in a terminal on the recipient's computer
curl -o KB-2026-004411.mlep "<the download link>"
What came back
(a file of 2372 bytes is saved, and nothing is printed)
Typed by Ruth, in a terminal on the recipient's computer
python open_legal_package.py KB-2026-004411.mlep --out opened --public-key <the platform's public key> --passphrase <the passphrase>
What came back
OK: 1 file for matter HC-2026-0417 (demand KB-2026-004411, produced 2026-10-10T19:03:29.245302+00:00). Signature verified.
The program prints one line, beginning OK: 1 file for matter HC-2026-0417 and ending Signature verified. A wrong passphrase, a changed byte, a file cut short or a key that is not the platform’s each make it print a problem instead.
15
Ruth Aldous
Ruth looks at what the package holds
Terminal · on the recipient’s computer

Besides the one data file, the package holds the manifest and its signature, the chain of custody, the audit trail, and a list of records that no longer exist. The chain of custody is the record of who asked, who approved and who confirmed, and when, and for a filtered table it also names the values the custodian supplied. The audit trail is the list of who was allowed or refused what for the named dataset, as the demand asked.

What the folder opened now holds
audit-trail.csv   68 bytes
chain-of-custody.json   1591 bytes
data/appointments/v1/v1.filtered.csv   199 bytes
erased.json   77 bytes
manifest.json   1123 bytes
manifest.sig   128 bytes
The listing shows audit-trail.csv, chain-of-custody.json, erased.json, manifest.json, manifest.sig and one file under data/appointments/v1.
16
Ruth Aldous
The table holds only the claimant’s rows
Terminal · on the recipient’s computer

The clinic’s table has ten rows for five patients. The package holds the two that match the patient id the custodian named, with every column kept, and nothing about the other four patients. The platform does not decide what is private or privileged beyond that. It copies the matching rows exactly, and the manifest records how the file was made: the column, how many values were named, how many rows matched out of how many, and the fingerprint of the sealed records they were taken from.

What the file opened/data/appointments/v1/v1.filtered.csv holds
"appointment_id","patient_id","patient_name","appointment_on","reason"
"A-0001","P-4471","Ms Alder","2026-03-04","Follow-up consultation"
"A-0004","P-4471","Ms Alder","2026-04-09","Procedure review"
The file has a header line and two rows, A-0001 and A-0004, both for P-4471, Ms Alder. No row of Mr Bellamy, Ms Carrow, Mr Dalton or Ms Everett is present.
